exercises.title: Hear Where the Blues Starts
exercises.instructions: 1. Count 1–2–3–4 while listening to or imagining a 12-measure blues. 2. Clap at measures 1, 5, and 9; these start three groups of four measures. 3. Start again at measure 1. Goal: Notice when each new group begins. A group of measures is called a phrase.

exercises.title: Feel the Swing Beat
exercises.instructions: 1. Count 1–2–3–4 at a comfortable speed. 2. Clap on counts 2 and 4, keeping 1 and 3 silent. 3. Play even quarter notes, then try pairs of swung eighth notes (long–short). Goal: Keep a steady beat for one minute.

exercises.title: Play and Explore the F Blues Scale
exercises.instructions: 1. Slowly play F, A♭, B♭, B, C, E♭, F, then come back down. 2. Use a few of those notes to play a short musical question. 3. Answer it with another short phrase. Goal: Create two different phrases from the same notes. This note set is the F blues scale.

exercises.title: Find the Starting Note of Each Chord
exercises.instructions: 1. Look at the chart and name the first note in each chord: F7 starts on F, B♭7 on B♭, and C7 on C. 2. Sing each starting note, then play it. 3. Repeat without looking. Goal: Recognize each chord's root note by ear.

exercises.title: Practice the Important Notes in Each Chord
exercises.instructions: 1. Play the 3rd and 7th of Dm7 (F and C). 2. Move to G7 (B and F), then Cmaj7 (E and B). 3. Move each note as little as possible. Goal: Connect all three chords smoothly. These notes are called guide tones; the chord sequence is ii–V–I.

exercises.title: Play the Notes of Each Chord
exercises.instructions: 1. Play Dm7 as D–F–A–C, one note at a time, up and down. 2. Do the same for G7 (G–B–D–F) and Cmaj7 (C–E–G–B). 3. Repeat slowly without stopping. Goal: Hear all four notes of each chord. Playing chord notes separately is called an arpeggio.

exercises.title: Make a Solo from Chord Notes
exercises.instructions: 1. Choose the F blues chart. 2. Play only the root, 3rd, 5th, or 7th of the chord shown in each measure. 3. Pause between short phrases. Goal: Play through all 12 measures once. The 12-measure round is called a chorus.

exercises.title: Play a Musical Question and Answer
exercises.instructions: 1. Play a short two-measure phrase. 2. Leave two beats of silence. 3. Play a similar phrase that sounds like an answer. Goal: Make three different question-and-answer pairs. Musicians also call this call and response.
exercises.suggested_material: F blues, no melody recording required

exercises.title: Count Through a 12-Bar Blues
exercises.instructions: 1. Count four beats in each measure from 1 to 12. 2. Clap on beats 2 and 4. 3. Notice the change to B♭7 at measure 5 and the ending chords in measures 11–12. Goal: Find your way back to measure 1 without losing count. This repeating pattern is the blues form.

exercises.title: Rootless Guide-Tone Shells
exercises.instructions: On piano or guitar, voice just 3rd and 7th of each ii–V–I chord. Keep movement minimal; bass can play roots separately.

exercises.title: Motif and Rhythmic Variation
exercises.instructions: Improvise a two-bar motif, then repeat it with a changed rhythm, preserving one recognizable interval or accent.

exercises.title: Transcribe a Four-Bar Phrase
exercises.instructions: Listen to an authorized recording. Sing a four-bar phrase, locate pitches slowly, then reproduce the rhythm without sheet music.
exercises.suggested_material: Bring your own licensed audio; no default recording

exercises.title: Walk from One Chord to the Next
exercises.instructions: 1. Play one note on each of the four beats. 2. Start each new chord with its root, such as F for F7. 3. On beat 4, choose a note one step away from the next chord's root. Goal: Connect four measures without stopping. A steady four-note line is called walking bass.

exercises.title: Comping with Space
exercises.instructions: Play sparse 2–4 note voicings with clear rests. Avoid constant quarter-note attacks; listen for where a soloist could breathe.

exercises.title: Build a One-Chorus Solo
exercises.instructions: Chorus 1: rhythmic motif. Chorus 2: guide-tone targets. Chorus 3: combine, leaving at least one full bar of rest. Record a note afterward.

exercises.title: Learn a Short Melody by Listening
exercises.instructions: 1. Play a short original or personally provided four-measure melody. 2. Sing it back before touching your instrument. 3. Find the notes by ear, then try them in two keys. Goal: Play the full phrase without reading notes.

exercises.title: Hear the Low Notes in a Song
exercises.instructions: 1. Choose a recording you have permission to use. 2. Listen only to the low bass part. 3. Hum its first note when each chord changes. Goal: Hear and follow four chord changes. The starting note of a chord is its root.

exercises.title: Play Freely for Three Minutes
exercises.instructions: 1. Pick a rhythm or a few notes that sound good to you. 2. Make up short phrases without worrying about mistakes. 3. When you finish, name one sound you liked. Goal: Explore a new musical idea.

exercises.title: Hear the Chord Changes in B♭ Blues
exercises.instructions: 1. Count three groups of four measures in the B♭ blues chart. 2. Say the first note of each chord aloud. 3. Play its 3rd, then create a short two-measure phrase. Goal: Stay oriented through all 12 measures. The first note is the chord root.

exercises.title: Rhythm Changes: Hear the Bridge
exercises.instructions: Play the A-section progression once, then isolate bars 17–24. Follow D7 → G7 → C7 → F7 roots and return to the A section.

exercises.title: Connect Chords in a Gentle Bossa
exercises.instructions: 1. Choose the 16-measure C minor bossa chart and play slowly with even eighth notes. 2. For each chord, play its 3rd and 7th. 3. Repeat measures 9–12 before playing all 16. Goal: Change chords without stopping. These important notes are called guide tones; bossa has a relaxed Brazilian rhythm.
exercises.suggested_material: Minor Bossa in C Minor (16-bar Study)

exercises.title: Hear the Move from Major to Minor
exercises.instructions: 1. Look at the 16-measure major-to-minor chord study. 2. Play each chord's starting note (root), then its 3rd and 7th. 3. Listen for the change from G major to E minor. Goal: Keep a slow, steady pulse across eight measures. The 3rd and 7th are guide tones.

exercises.title: Make a Two-Note Musical Idea
exercises.instructions: 1. Choose two notes from D, E, F, G, A, B, C. 2. Play them as a short pattern, then repeat with a new rhythm and a pause. 3. When the chart moves up one semitone, move your two notes up one semitone too. Goal: Create a recognizable idea with space between phrases. This is modal improvisation.
exercises.suggested_material: Two-Center Modal Study in D (16 bars)

exercises.title: Recognize ABAC Form
exercises.instructions: Mark the end of each 8-bar section. Compare bars 9–16 and 25–32, then improvise one chorus using only chord tones.

exercises.title: AABA: Track the Bridge
exercises.instructions: Count the four 8-bar sections out loud. In the bridge, play chord roots on beat 1 and seventh-to-third voice leading without stopping.

exercises.title: Compare Two Ways to Play a Minor Blues
exercises.instructions: 1. Play one round of the C minor blues using C, E♭, F, G, B♭. 2. Play another round using only notes from each displayed chord. 3. Listen closely at measures 9–10. Goal: Hear how the chord changes affect your note choices. Each round is a chorus.

exercises.title: Slow Ballad: Smooth Voice Leading
exercises.instructions: Keep the tempo slow. Play only third and seventh notes with minimal motion, leaving a beat of silence after each chord change.

routines.title: Make Your First Jazz Solo
routines.description: Count a blues, try a few scale notes, then make up short questions and answers.

routines.title: Daily Jazz Warm-Up
routines.description: Feel the beat, play the notes of a few chords, and finish with free play.

routines.title: Learn a 12-Bar Blues
routines.description: Count the blues pattern, hear the chord changes, and try your own short solo.

routines.title: Connect Three Common Jazz Chords
routines.description: Practice Dm7, G7, and Cmaj7 one step at a time. Jazz players call this ii–V–I.

routines.title: Play with Steady Swing Rhythm
routines.description: Keep a steady beat, practice musical questions and answers, and play freely.

routines.title: Develop Longer Jazz Solos
routines.description: Learn a short phrase by ear, vary rhythms, and connect chord tones through the blues.

routines.title: Walking Bass: Start with Four Beats
routines.description: Find chord roots, play one note per beat, and walk through the blues.

routines.title: Leave Space When Playing Chords
routines.description: Practice sparse chord accompaniment (comping) and responsive rhythms.

routines.title: Train Your Ear: Hear and Sing Notes
routines.description: Recognize where the blues begins, sing chord roots, and listen to the bass.

routines.title: Practice Without a Backing Track
routines.description: Use your own counting and a little free play to keep time confidently.

routines.title: Get Comfortable with Jazz Song Forms
routines.description: Listen for sections, follow a B♭ blues, and practice a major-to-minor chord change.

routines.title: Start Playing a Gentle Minor Bossa
routines.description: Learn relaxed bossa rhythm and connect the important notes of each chord.

routines.title: Follow the Sections of Rhythm Changes
routines.description: Keep swing time and learn to move through the contrasting bridge section.

routines.title: Explore Song Forms and Ballad Chords
routines.description: Practice ABAC forms, smooth chord movement, and two-note modal ideas.

paths.title: Your First Week of Jazz
paths.guidance: Seven suggested sessions, not consecutive-day requirements. Repeat any day. Short sessions count.

paths.title: Learn a Tune by Ear
paths.guidance: Use an original or rights-cleared tune. Hear → sing → changes → voice-lead → improvise.

paths.title: Better Swing and Time Feel
paths.guidance: Alternate 2-and-4 metronome, no-click phrases and playing with a band.
